Oscar Pistorius Probation: The process

By: Este de Klerk | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
In less than a week, Oscar Pistorius will be released under correctional supervision. He's served the ten months, as dictated by his sentence. But what is the process he had to undergo in prison?

Summary:
Almost all the media are incorrectly reporting that Oscar Pistorius will be released on parole.
This, of course, is wrong. He is not being released on parole, but under correctional supervision and there is a big difference.
According to the Criminal Procedures Act, when an offender is sentenced to five years or less, he or she only has to serve one sixth of the sentence behind bars. The other sixth of the sentence that would make up one third of the total sentence, could be served under correctional supervision - with conditions stipulated by the Department of Correctional Services.

Further information:
Oscar's placement under correctional supervision was a sentence of the court - with other words, there was never any doubt that he would serve longer than ten months in prison - if he adhered to all the rules and regulations in prison and had acted in good faith and behaviour - and there was never any doubt when Judge Masipa sentenced him that he would be placed under correctional supervision after serving only ten months. But prisoners still need to undergo certain programmes in prison, still need to see psychologists and criminologists in prison and this would all be taken into account when the Parole Board sit and decide whether to release an inmate or not.

When Correctional Services Commissioner, Zack Modise announced in June that Oscar Pistorius would be released under correctional supervision in August, he said Oscar had completed a number of courses - among them, seemingly one on anger management. Spokesperson Manelisi Wolela told SAFM the fact that Pistorius would be released under correctional supervision, was "evidence that the athlete's conduct while incarcerated had been acceptable and that he had been upgraded while serving his sentence".

The Department of Correctional Services has not yet made public the conditions of Pistorius's correctional supervision - they have not yet indicated where he would be kept while under house arrest, if he had to do some community service, what the conditions are.

But the Department's website give some general conditions of the normal provisions.

Offenders are normally confined to a certain area, so it is unlikely that there would be any overseas trips for Pistorius during this time. He won't be able to change his place of residence without consent. While under house arrest, offenders are permitted to "participate in organised sport activities, to attend church services, to do the necessary shopping etc."

He will have to report to the Community Corrections Office at set intervals, and will also be monitored by correctional officials who will pay visits to his house. He may have to complete some kind of community service or attend "specialised programmes or lectures on specific subjects. It is also unlikely that he would be able to drink any alcohol.

If Pistorius violates these conditions, he isn't automatically sent back to jail, but "serious or persistent violations of conditions", however, mean that he might have to serve the remainder of his sentence behind bars.

Already in the second week of June this year, Oscar would have began "release preparation", which is designed for non-compliance. It is also intended to assist him in "dealing with the sigma attached to imprisonment".

In this story, we will also look at what a Parole Board need to look at when they evaluate the readiness of an inmate to be release under parole or correctional supervision. There are 52 Parole Boards in the country. The victim's family can participate, either by appearing in person or by writing a letter or by supplying the Parole Board with a video message. Even though the victim's family's participation would be taken into consideration by the Parole Board, it wouldn't be the only factor that would be considered.

Reeva's parents, June and Barry wrote a letter to the Parole Board in which they said that ten months was not enough for the deed.

Correctional supervision is a community-based sentence which is served by the offender in the community under the control and supervision of correctional officials, subject to conditions which have been set by the court or the Commissioner of Correctional Services, in order to protect the community and to prevent relapse into crime.

There are very strict rules and regulations to which a prisoner placed under correctional supervision have to adhere to.

Press Release:


Oscar Probation
At the end of next week, Oscar Pistorius will be released from Kgosi Mampuru II prison having served 10 months of his 5-year sentence. Carte Blanche asks what life will be like for the Paralympian as he serves out the remainder of his sentence under correctional supervision? From strict monitoring of his movements by the Department of Correctional Services to media invasion of his privacy and regaining society’s acceptance, the road ahead for Oscar is set to be anything but a walk in the park.


Script:


OSCAR PROBATION

PRODUCER: ESTé DE KLERK

JUDGE MASIPA: The following is what I consider a sentence that is firm and just both to society and to the accused. Count 1: Culpable Homicide – the sentence imposed is a maximum imprisonment of five years imposed in terms of section 276 (1) (i) of the Criminal Procedure Act, number 51 of 1977.

Ten months ago Judge Thokozile Masipa sent Paralympian Oscar Pistorius to prison after 49 days on trial.

In real time, the legal proceedings - watched by millions around the globe - lasted seven months.

In the two and a half years since Oscar Pistorius shot and killed his girlfriend, Reeva Steenkamp, his life has changed irrevocably.

JUDGE MASIPA: A non-custodial sentence would send wrong sentence to community, on the other hand, a long sentence would also not be appropriate either as it would lack the element of mercy.

On the 21st of October last year Oscar began one of the most traumatic chapters of his life yet – ten months incarceration at the Kgosi Mampuru II prison in Pretoria.

DEVI LINK: Oscar was sentenced under section 276 (1) (i) of the Criminal Procedure Act, which means that if a sentence doesn’t exceed more than five years, then one sixth of that sentence must be served in prison before being considered for placement under correctional supervision.

On Friday, the 21st of August this year, exactly ten months later, another chapter will begin for the Paralympian. He will neither be imprisoned, nor will he be free.
The Act states that an offender has to serve the remainder of a sentence under correctional supervision, says defence attorney Cliffie Alexander.

CLIFFIE ALEXANDER: He will be released from Kgosi Mampuru II prison, that doesn’t mean he is being released, that he has served his sentence. It only means that you are going to continue serving the rest of your prison sentence at a given address and you are going to be very, very strictly monitored.

Monitored officially by the Department of Correctional Services, but unofficially, also by the community, says criminologist, Anni Hesselink, who has been working in South African prisons for the past 22 years.

DEVI: Correctional supervision, does it work?

ANNI HESSELINK: Yes it does, but it depends on the type of offender, the type of personality, the type of crime that’s been committed. In cases where its a once-off crime that’s been committed and the person is really dedicated to change and there is no denial, there is remorse, there is victim empathy, then of course it’s a very good option.

The NPA’s appeal against Judge Masipa’s verdict is set to be heard in the Supreme Court of Appeal in November. But for now, Oscar is set to be under correctional supervision for four years and two months says Manelisi Wolela, spokesperson for the Department of Correctional Services.

DEVI: People have this idea that come the 21st of August, Oscar is going to be a free man?

MANELISI WOLELA: You are still an offender until your full sentence is completed and therefore when you are placed either parole or community corrections as a probationer there are conditions you have got to meet, which may include house arrest, your movement is curtailed, you are checked periodically, sometimes at randomly and all those things and therefore you are not a free man, you become a free man when you’ve completed your sentence.

CLIFFIE ALEXANDER: It is a very, very serious form of, call it imprisonment per se, there is absolutely no doubt about that.

ANNI HESSELINK: Especially if it’s a high profile case - your life is open to everyone to scrutinize, to report, to evaluate.

Strict conditions dictate correctional supervision or parole. These are rules and regulations offenders need to sign for and ad-here to.
But ad-hering to strict conditions is far better than being incarcerated, says dr. Lorinda Bergh. She’s worked for Correctional Services for thirty years and was the national director of psychologists for seventeen of those.

DR. LORINDA BERGH: Every offender that I have ever spoken to will tell you the most important thing for me in prison was getting back my freedom, when I can put off my own lights, where I can go to, what I can eat, that I can be with my family, that I can see my children.

The department won’t divulge the stipulated conditions around Oscar’s correctional supervision or where he will be staying while under house arrest.

MANELISI WOLELA: General conditions include issues of house arrest, include you must not commit crime, the abuse of alcohol, you know threatening victims and a range of those.

Prisoner turned motivational speaker, Thabo Nkosi from Tembisa, east of Joburg, says being on parole is imprisonment in your own home. Thabo has been on parole since 2013, after serving seven and a half years of a fifteen-year sentence for armed robbery.

THABO NKOSI: You are limited. It feels like you are still in prison. You are still being bound by correctional services.

Thabo has between two to six hours per day either to seek work, go shopping or enjoy free time. He feels that adhering to parole conditions is serving a sentence outside prison. His parole ends in 2020.

THABO: Those people have a right to go inside your room, inside your house and search for anything that is illegal, so that if they find that particular thing, then you go back to prison.

Besides possibly having to find employment, Oscar will also have to do community service.

Cliffie: You remember that Mr Gerrie Nel advocated the argument that he didn’t have full time employment per se, which is one of the conditions. The counter argument from the defence is that but he's and athlete, earns money via being a professional athlete. Community service also comes in, you will remember that evidence was lead that he would love to work with children. Children would love him, he has got a lot of knowledge to impart.

Being back in the community will open Oscar up to public scrutiny. And Thabo says it takes a lot to prove yourself again to people who have cast you aside.

THABO NKOSI: The minute they hear about me being in prison and all that, they don’t trust you anymore. Like, myself, they know, here in the yard, that I was the one who was arrested, and if something is lost here, I am the first suspect.

DEVI: You took it?

THABO: I took it.

DR. LORINDA BERGH: It’s always a traumatic transition. It takes them quite a while to really adapt to the prison and then before they get released from prison they get very traumatised again and very anxious, because now I am going back to the community - what is being expected by me by the community? How are they going to deal with me?

Oscar’s physical disability saw him incarcerated in a single cell in the hospital section of the prison.

CLIFFIE ALEXANDER: There is absolutely no doubt that he did not have an easy time. You cannot come and go as you please. He has got no freedom of movement. Imagine being taken out of your comfort zone, although you have been found guilty, so you don’t deserve to be in a comfort zone, per se, but you are put into a specific place, you don’t get to eat the food of your choice, being an athlete which is very, very important. You get fed what everybody else get’s fed. You stand in a cue like everybody else stands in a cue.

The last images the world saw of Oscar after he was sentenced were of him being led down the courtroom stairs.
But in March a leaked amateur video showed Oscar and Czech fugitive Radovan Krejir playing football in the prison courtyard. Oscar and Radovan are both held in the single cell hospital ward of the prison.

DEVI: How did the department feel when the footage of Oscar Pistorious and Radovan Krejir was released?

MANELISI: The concern, of course which we will always have, is the ongoing challenge of smuggling into our facilities of cellphones. We have stated very clearly, even at that stage, that number one, we encourage optimal participation of offenders in all sorts of forms of sport. In some instances it contributes in their sense of self-worth.

And a sense of self-worth is important in rehabilitation, says dr. Bergh.

DR. LORINDA BERGH: You will either come out worse or you will come out better, but the decision is yours. Your own behaviour is going to indicate where you are going to go to. If you attend the programmes and you really show the correctional officials that you are doing the right things, you respect what they do, you respect the norms and the values of the system, because that’s why you were sent there, you didn’t respect the norms and values of society.

While in prison, offenders are given the opportunity to enroll in various courses to aid in rehabilitating their offending behaviour. But doing so is not compulsory.
Oscar has completed two courses.

MANELISI: We can confirm that he has gone through the intervention programmes that were implemented, short intervention programmes that were implemented over the period. One of them being anger management and the other one is cross roads. Cross roads is essentially about how you are assisted to further with clarity differentiate between that which is wrong and that which is right.

Aside from the programmes, input from the victim’s family is also considered by the Parole Board.

DEVI LINK: June and Barry Steenkamp wrote a letter to the Parole Board. In this letter they say while they have forgiven Oscar, incarceration of ten months is not enough for taking a life.

MANELISI: Before the decision was made a request was sent to the family for the family to come and participate in the process and as you probably know, the family sent a letter to say they don’t want to participate in that process physically.

Ten weeks before an offender’s release, they start a pre-release program to prepare them to rejoin the community.

Thabo’s advise to Oscar? Walk the straight and narrow.

THABO NKOSI: It is not going to be easy, but he needs to hang in there. He should go to the Steenkamp-family, irrespective of whether they welcome him or not, you understand, but he must do it wholeheartedly.

CLIFFIE ALEXANDER: He is going to be reintegrated slowly back into public. Let him impart the knowledge and the experiences that he has gained to younger people, so hopefully they don’t make the same mistake.

DEVI: What can Oscar Pistorious expect under correctional supervision?

ANNI: He will have to keep himself composed in all types of situations and scenarios, a lot of self control, be courteous to everyone, because he will be provoked, he will have no privacy, he will be followed, being such a high profile person, being so well known, being a real celebrity in South Africa and worldwide. It’s really, really not going to be easy for him.

STUDIO OUTRO:
The Department of Correctional Services has not yet announced when on Friday Oscar Pistorius would be released from the Kgosi Mampuru II prison.


PROMO’S

PROMO 1: 15”

Strict conditions are set to dictate Oscar Pistorius’s life once he is released under correctional supervision on Friday.

CLIFFIE ALEXANDER: It only means that you are going to continue serving the rest of your prison sentence at a given address and you are going to be very, very strictly monitored.

PROMO 2: 15
DEVI LINK: Soon to be released under correctional supervision, what does the future hold for Oscar Pistorius?

ANNI HESSELINK: He will be provoked, he will have no privacy, he will be followed. It’s really, really not going to be easy for him.

PROMO 3: 10”
DEVI LINK: What will living under correctional supervision be like for Paralympian, Oscar Pistorius?

ANNI: Your life is open to everyone to scrutinise, to report, to evaluate.

Imagine being taken out of your comfort zone, although you have been found guilty, so you don’t deserve to be in a comfort zone, per se, but you are put into a specific place, you don’t get to eat the food of your choice, being an athlete which is very, very important. You get fed what everybody else get’s fed. You stand in a cue like everybody else stands in a cue. The last images the world saw of Oscar after he was sentenced were of him being led down the courtroom stairs. But in March a leaked amateur video showed Oscar and Czech fugitive Radovan Krejir playing football in the prison courtyard. Oscar and Radovan are both held in the single cell hospital ward of the prison. DEVI: How did the department feel when the footage of Oscar Pistorious and Radovan Krejir was released? MANELISI: The concern, of course which we will always have, is the ongoing challenge of smuggling into our facilities of cellphones. We have stated very clearly, even at that stage, that number one, we encourage optimal participation of offenders in all sorts of forms of sport. In some instances it contributes in their sense of self-worth. And a sense of self-worth is important in rehabilitation, says dr. Bergh. DR. LORINDA BERGH: You will either come out worse or you will come out better, but the decision is yours. Your own behaviour is going to indicate where you are going to go to. If you attend the programmes and you really show the correctional officials that you are doing the right things, you respect what they do, you respect the norms and the values of the system, because that’s why you were sent there, you didn’t respect the norms and values of society. While in prison, offenders are given the opportunity to enroll in various courses to aid in rehabilitating their offending behaviour. But doing so is not compulsory. Oscar has completed two courses. MANELISI: We can confirm that he has gone through the intervention programmes that were implemented, short intervention programmes that were implemented over the period. One of them being anger management and the other one is cross roads. Cross roads is essentially about how you are assisted to further with clarity differentiate between that which is wrong and that which is right. Aside from the programmes, input from the victim’s family is also considered by the Parole Board. DEVI LINK: June and Barry Steenkamp wrote a letter to the Parole Board. In this letter they say while they have forgiven Oscar, incarceration of ten months is not enough for taking a life. MANELISI: Before the decision was made a request was sent to the family for the family to come and participate in the process and as you probably know, the family sent a letter to say they don’t want to participate in that process physically. Ten weeks before an offender’s release, they start a pre-release program to prepare them to rejoin the community. Thabo’s advise to Oscar? Walk the straight and narrow. THABO NKOSI: It is not going to be easy, but he needs to hang in there. He should go to the Steenkamp-family, irrespective of whether they welcome him or not, you understand, but he must do it wholeheartedly. CLIFFIE ALEXANDER: He is going to be reintegrated slowly back into public. Let him impart the knowledge and the experiences that he has gained to younger people, so hopefully they don’t make the same mistake. DEVI: What can Oscar Pistorious expect under correctional supervision? ANNI: He will have to keep himself composed in all types of situations and scenarios, a lot of self control, be courteous to everyone, because he will be provoked, he will have no privacy, he will be followed, being such a high profile person, being so well known, being a real celebrity in South Africa and worldwide. It’s really, really not going to be easy for him. STUDIO OUTRO: The Department of Correctional Services has not yet announced when on Friday Oscar Pistorius would be released from the Kgosi Mampuru II prison. PROMO’S PROMO 1: 15” Strict conditions are set to dictate Oscar Pistorius’s life once he is released under correctional supervision on Friday. CLIFFIE ALEXANDER: It only means that you are going to continue serving the rest of your prison sentence at a given address and you are going to be very, very strictly monitored. PROMO 2: 15 DEVI LINK: Soon to be released under correctional supervision, what does the future hold for Oscar Pistorius? ANNI HESSELINK: He will be provoked, he will have no privacy, he will be followed. It’s really, really not going to be easy for him. PROMO 3: 10” DEVI LINK: What will living under correctional supervision be like for Paralympian, Oscar Pistorius? ANNI: Your life is open to everyone to scrutinise, to report, to evaluate. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): In less than a week, Oscar Pistorius will be released under correctional supervision. He's served the ten months, as dictated by his sentence. But what is the process he had to undergo in prison?
metadata.Summary: Almost all the media are incorrectly reporting that Oscar Pistorius will be released on parole. This, of course, is wrong. He is not being released on parole, but under correctional supervision and there is a big difference. According to the Criminal Procedures Act, when an offender is sentenced to five years or less, he or she only has to serve one sixth of the sentence behind bars. The other sixth of the sentence that would make up one third of the total sentence, could be served under correctional supervision - with conditions stipulated by the Department of Correctional Services.
metadata.Further information: Oscar's placement under correctional supervision was a sentence of the court - with other words, there was never any doubt that he would serve longer than ten months in prison - if he adhered to all the rules and regulations in prison and had acted in good faith and behaviour - and there was never any doubt when Judge Masipa sentenced him that he would be placed under correctional supervision after serving only ten months. But prisoners still need to undergo certain programmes in prison, still need to see psychologists and criminologists in prison and this would all be taken into account when the Parole Board sit and decide whether to release an inmate or not. When Correctional Services Commissioner, Zack Modise announced in June that Oscar Pistorius would be released under correctional supervision in August, he said Oscar had completed a number of courses - among them, seemingly one on anger management. Spokesperson Manelisi Wolela told SAFM the fact that Pistorius would be released under correctional supervision, was "evidence that the athlete's conduct while incarcerated had been acceptable and that he had been upgraded while serving his sentence". The Department of Correctional Services has not yet made public the conditions of Pistorius's correctional supervision - they have not yet indicated where he would be kept while under house arrest, if he had to do some community service, what the conditions are. But the Department's website give some general conditions of the normal provisions. Offenders are normally confined to a certain area, so it is unlikely that there would be any overseas trips for Pistorius during this time. He won't be able to change his place of residence without consent. While under house arrest, offenders are permitted to "participate in organised sport activities, to attend church services, to do the necessary shopping etc." He will have to report to the Community Corrections Office at set intervals, and will also be monitored by correctional officials who will pay visits to his house. He may have to complete some kind of community service or attend "specialised programmes or lectures on specific subjects. It is also unlikely that he would be able to drink any alcohol. If Pistorius violates these conditions, he isn't automatically sent back to jail, but "serious or persistent violations of conditions", however, mean that he might have to serve the remainder of his sentence behind bars. Already in the second week of June this year, Oscar would have began "release preparation", which is designed for non-compliance. It is also intended to assist him in "dealing with the sigma attached to imprisonment". In this story, we will also look at what a Parole Board need to look at when they evaluate the readiness of an inmate to be release under parole or correctional supervision. There are 52 Parole Boards in the country. The victim's family can participate, either by appearing in person or by writing a letter or by supplying the Parole Board with a video message. Even though the victim's family's participation would be taken into consideration by the Parole Board, it wouldn't be the only factor that would be considered. Reeva's parents, June and Barry wrote a letter to the Parole Board in which they said that ten months was not enough for the deed. Correctional supervision is a community-based sentence which is served by the offender in the community under the control and supervision of correctional officials, subject to conditions which have been set by the court or the Commissioner of Correctional Services, in order to protect the community and to prevent relapse into crime. There are very strict rules and regulations to which a prisoner placed under correctional supervision have to adhere to.
